what_its_for: Nivolumab is a cancer medicine called an immunotherapy drug. It works by helping your own immune system find and attack cancer cells. It is used to treat several types of cancer, including melanoma (skin cancer), lung cancer, kidney cancer, bladder cancer, certain head and neck cancers, liver cancer, colon cancer, stomach cancer, and others. Your doctor chose this medicine because it may help slow or stop your cancer from growing.
how_to_take: Nivolumab is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or port at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. Each infusion usually takes about 30 to 60 minutes. A healthcare professional will give you every dose. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the type of cancer being treated. Most people receive nivolumab every 2, 4, or 6 weeks, depending on the treatment plan. Common doses are 240 mg every 2 weeks, 480 mg every 4 weeks, or 3 mg per kilogram (kg) of body weight every 2 weeks, but your dose may be different. Always follow your doctor's exact schedule. Do not skip or change your appointments without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to set up a new appointment as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your healthcare team will tell you the best time to get your next infusion and will adjust your schedule if needed.
storage: You do not need to store nivolumab at home because it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals at a clinic or hospital. If for any reason you are given a supply to bring to another facility, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in its original packaging and protected from light. Do not shake the vial. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving any live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax or yellow fever vaccine) while you are being treated with nivolumab, as they could be harmful. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child during treatment, as nivolumab can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose. Tell all of your doctors and pharmacists that you are on nivolumab before starting any new medicines, including herbal supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Nivolumab works by boosting your immune system, which can sometimes cause your immune system to attack healthy parts of your body. Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of these warning signs: new or worsening cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath (could signal lung problems); severe diarrhea, stomach pain, or blood in your stool (could signal bowel problems); yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe nausea (could signal liver problems); severe headache, confusion, or vision changes (could signal brain or nerve problems); muscle weakness or joint pain (could signal muscle or joint inflammation); rash, blistering, or peeling skin (could signal a serious skin reaction); frequent urination, increased thirst, or extreme fatigue (could signal hormone or kidney problems); any signs of infection such as fever or chills. These side effects can happen at any time during treatment or even after it ends. Never ignore a new or unusual symptom — always call your doctor to be safe.
when_it_works: Nivolumab does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before you and your doctor can see if it is helping. Some people respond quickly, while others take longer. Your doctor will order regular scans and blood tests to check how well the medicine is working. Even if you feel the same or have side effects early on, this does not always mean the medicine is not working. Stay patient, keep all of your appointments, and talk honestly with your doctor about how you are feeling.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use nivolumab if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant, as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 5 months after stopping. Children: Nivolumab may be used in some children 12 years and older for certain conditions; your child's doctor will decide if it is appropriate. Older adults (age 65 and older): Nivolumab can generally be used in older adults, but they may need to be watched more closely for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems before starting treatment, as this medicine may affect these organs and may require closer monitoring.
